analysis.one_liner: Requires hospitals and nursing homes to report deaths and injuries from medical devices and lets the FDA order recalls.
analysis.headline: Passed both the House and Senate by voice vote and was signed into law on November 28, 1990, as Public Law 101-629.
analysis.plain_summary: This law requires hospitals, nursing homes, outpatient treatment facilities, and surgical centers to report to federal health officials and device makers whenever a medical device probably caused or contributed to a death, illness, or injury. It requires manufacturers to track certain devices so patients can be notified of problems, gives the Food and Drug Administration power to order recalls of dangerous devices, and requires monitoring of newly introduced devices after they reach the market. It also tightens the review process for devices that claim to be copies of already-approved products.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who receive implanted or other medical devices, and their families. When a device injures or kills someone, the problem now gets reported to regulators and the manufacturer, devices can be tracked so patients can be warned, and the FDA can order a recall of a device it finds likely to cause serious harm or death.

how_it_helps.text: Hospitals, nursing homes, ambulatory surgical facilities, and outpatient treatment facilities must report to the Secretary of Health and Human Services, the manufacturer, or both whenever they believe a device probably caused or contributed to a death, illness, or injury.

Manufacturers must adopt a method of device tracking, and the FDA may order that a device cease distribution and that health professionals and facilities be notified when it finds a reasonable probability of serious adverse health consequences or death.

Manufacturers must conduct postmarket surveillance of certain devices first introduced after January 1, 1991, under an FDA-approved protocol, so problems show up after sale rather than being caught only in premarket testing.

A device can only be treated as a copy of an approved device if it has the same intended use and either the same technological characteristics or data showing it is as safe and effective as a legally marketed device, and manufacturers of certain such devices must certify they searched for and summarized all adverse safety and effectiveness data.
The FDA may temporarily suspend, as well as withdraw, approval of a device's premarket application, and may initiate reclassification of devices itself rather than waiting for manufacturers.

analysis.who_pays: Medical device manufacturers, importers, and distributors bear the cost of reporting, recordkeeping, device tracking, and postmarket surveillance, and face stricter premarket review. Hospitals, nursing homes, and other device user facilities bear new reporting duties and paperwork. Some of those costs can be passed on through device prices and facility billing.

drawbacks.text: The civil penalties for failing to report only take effect if the Secretary of Health and Human Services concludes, in a study due 48 months after enactment, that facilities have not substantially complied — so enforcement is back-loaded and conditional.

A facility's report of a device-related death, illness, or injury generally cannot be used in a civil lawsuit between private parties unless the person who made the report knew it was false, which limits the report's usefulness to injured patients suing over a faulty device.

Recall orders do not include recall from individuals, and do not include recall from facilities where recalling the device poses a greater health risk than leaving it in use — so patients may keep a defective implanted device.

The reporting, recordkeeping, and tracking duties add administrative costs for hospitals, nursing homes, and device companies, and new requirements come with a humanitarian-device exemption pathway that allows devices for rare conditions (fewer than 4,000 patients) to skip standard effectiveness requirements.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety gains are real: mandatory reporting closes a gap in which device-related deaths and injuries often never reached regulators, and recall and tracking powers address cases where patients with implanted devices could not be warned. The costs are mostly administrative, spread across manufacturers and facilities. The main honest criticism is that Congress softened the enforcement teeth — penalties are conditional on a future compliance study, and facility reports are shielded from most lawsuits — so the law leans on voluntary compliance more than its supporters might have preferred.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared committee in October 1990, passed the House and Senate by voice vote, was worked out in a conference between the two chambers, and the President signed it on November 28, 1990.

narrative.text: Rep. Henry Waxman introduced the Safe Medical Devices Act on August 2, 1989, and it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee.
The bill sat in the Health and the Environment Subcommittee until hearings in July 1990 and markup in September 1990, then was reported amended by the full committee on October 5, 1990.
The House passed the bill by voice vote under suspension of the rules on October 10, 1990.

The Senate passed its own version by voice vote on October 12, 1990, substituting the language of S. 3006, and appointed conferees including Democrats Kennedy, Pell, Metzenbaum, and Dodd and Republicans Hatch, Durenberger, and Coats.

The conference report was agreed to by voice vote in both the House and Senate on October 27, 1990, and the bill was presented to the President on November 19 and signed on November 28, 1990, becoming Public Law 101-629.

In the final version, civil penalties for facilities that knowingly fail to report take effect only if a later study finds substantial noncompliance, and facility reports are largely shielded from use in private civil actions.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Patients gained mandatory reporting, device tracking, and FDA recall authority they did not have before. Device manufacturers also came out relatively well: the conference version delayed penalties until a compliance study found noncompliance, shielded facility reports from most lawsuits, and added pathways such as the humanitarian-device exemption and sharing of premarket approval data after the fourth device of a kind.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Patients, with device makers making concessions

for.name: Rep. Henry Waxman
for.role: Chair, Health and the Environment Subcommittee, House Energy and Commerce
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill, moved to suspend the rules and pass it, requested the conference, and moved to agree to the conference report.

for.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
for.role: Standing committee with jurisdiction over food and drug law
for.what_they_did: Held subcommittee hearings and markup, ordered the bill reported amended, and filed the committee report (H. Rept. 101-808).

for.name: Senate conferees (Kennedy, Pell, Metzenbaum, Dodd, Hatch, Durenberger, Coats)
for.role: Senate conference committee on the bill
for.what_they_did: Negotiated the final version after the Senate passed its own language, which the House then agreed to conference on.

for.name: President George H.W. Bush
for.what_they_did: Signed the bill into law on November 28, 1990, as Public Law 101-629.

against.name: Medical device manufacturers
against.what_they_did: Opposed or sought to soften new reporting, tracking, and recall mandates and stricter review of copycat devices; the final law delays civil penalties until a compliance study and shields facility reports from most lawsuits.

sides.party_line_note: Both chambers passed the bill and the conference report by voice vote with no recorded opposition, and the Senate conferees included four Democrats and three Republicans; a Republican president signed it into law.

industries.note: The law imposes mandatory injury reporting, device tracking, recall orders, postmarket surveillance, and stricter review of devices claiming to copy approved ones — real oversight costs. But it also locks in concessions the industry sought: penalties only start after a compliance study finds noncompliance, a humanitarian-device exemption lets rare-disease devices skip effectiveness testing, and premarket data can be reused after the fourth device of a kind, speeding later approvals.

industries.industry: Hospitals, nursing homes, and outpatient treatment facilities
industries.note: These device user facilities take on mandatory reporting of device-related deaths, illnesses, and injuries, plus related recordkeeping. The cost is administrative, and the reporting directly serves patient safety, so their interest here runs alongside patients'.

They must certify annually how many reports they filed, maintain records, and report corrections or removals of devices undertaken to reduce health risks. The burden is compliance paperwork in service of a safety system patients rely on.
